article.headline: Congress’s $200 Secret: Late Trades, No Consequences
article.lede: Representative Julia Letlow of Louisiana filed over 210 stock trades months — in some cases more than a year — past their legal disclosure deadline, including a lucrative position in Micron Technology that has since surged by several hundred percent. The penalty she faces: a $200 fine that the House Ethics Committee has already voted to waive.
article.body:
The *Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act* — universally shortened to the STOCK Act — was signed into law in 2012 with considerable fanfare. Its premise was simple: members of Congress, soaking daily in market-moving information about legislation, regulations, and federal contracts, should at minimum be required to disclose their personal stock trades promptly. The law set a 45-day window for disclosure after any transaction. The fine for blowing past that window: two hundred dollars. Not per day of delay. Per report. As deterrents go, it ranks somewhere below a parking ticket in a city that doesn't tow.

Rep. Letlow, a Republican representing Louisiana's 5th congressional district who sits on the House Appropriations Committee — the body that controls federal spending — disclosed more than 210 individual stock and bond transactions in January 2026, many of them over a year late. The combined value of the trades is estimated at between $225,000 and $3.3 million. Among the positions was a purchase of Micron Technology ($MU), a semiconductor company whose fortunes have been transformed by the artificial-intelligence memory boom, made in April of the preceding year. Since that purchase, Micron's share price has risen by a figure that various trackers place in the range of 370 to 376 percent. Letlow's office attributed the late filings to her Merrill Lynch investment manager, who exercises *discretionary authority* — meaning he buys and sells without seeking her approval — and allegedly failed to flag that each transaction triggered a separate reporting obligation. She says she filed all the paperwork herself once she became aware of the problem.

The explanation is not implausible. Blind trusts and discretionary accounts are common in Washington precisely to create distance between lawmakers and their portfolios. But critics note that the obligation to file rests squarely on the member, not the broker. Senator Bill Cassidy, Letlow's opponent in Louisiana's 2026 Republican Senate primary, pointed to at least one trade executed within 48 hours of a subcommittee hearing — a detail that the discretionary-manager defense does not obviously cover. State Treasurer John Fleming was blunter: the responsibility, he said, lies with the member, not the adviser.

The larger story, however, is not about one congresswoman but about a decade-long failure of institutional design. Quiver Quantitative, an *alternative-data* firm (one that aggregates non-traditional datasets for investors and journalists) that scrapes STOCK Act filings and publishes them in searchable form, has documented that late disclosures are emphatically not a partisan phenomenon. In 2025 alone, Oregon Democrat Val Hoyle missed deadlines on 217 trades; California Democrat Linda Sánchez violated the 45-day rule as recently as January 2026; and a Campaign Legal Center tally found at least 17 lawmakers on both sides of the aisle in violation since July 2025. No member of Congress has ever been criminally prosecuted under the STOCK Act. The Ethics Committees of both chambers routinely waive even the nominal $200 charge — as the House committee did in Letlow's case.

The timing matters for reasons beyond the Senate race. Micron has become one of the canonical AI-era trades: the company is one of only three global suppliers of *HBM* (high-bandwidth memory), the stacked chip architecture required by the graphics processors that power large language models. With HBM demand sold out for several quarters by Micron's own account, its share price has been on an extraordinary run, reaching new 52-week highs in early May 2026 with some analysts projecting a price target of $1,000. A lawmaker who sits on the Appropriations Committee — which funds the very agencies shaping AI procurement and export-control policy — and who holds an undisclosed position in the sector's prime beneficiary is, at minimum, a case study in why the disclosure regime exists.

Congress has debated a full trading ban for years. A bipartisan bill, the *PELOSI Act* (named, with pointed irony, after the former Speaker whose husband's trades generated their own headlines), and various other reform proposals have come and gone without reaching a floor vote. Letlow herself now says she supports legislation banning members from trading individual stocks — a conversion that, given the circumstances of its announcement, her primary opponents have greeted with visible skepticism. The Appropriations subcommittee seat, the Merrill Lynch account, the April Micron buy, the year-plus delay, the $200 fine, the waiver: each element on its own is defensible, or at least deniable. Together they describe a system designed less to prevent conflicts of interest than to create the appearance of having thought about them.

concepts.definition: The Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act (2012), which requires members of Congress and their staff to publicly disclose personal stock trades within 45 days of execution. The civil penalty for a late filing is $200, a figure widely criticized as insufficient to deter violations.

A high-performance chip architecture that stacks multiple layers of DRAM vertically to dramatically increase data throughput. HBM is a critical component in the GPUs used to train and run large AI models, making its producers — Micron, SK Hynix, and Samsung — central players in the AI infrastructure buildout.

An arrangement in which an investor grants a financial adviser or investment manager the legal power to buy and sell securities on their behalf without seeking approval for each transaction. Common among public officials seeking to distance themselves from investment decisions, though it does not transfer the legal obligation to file STOCK Act disclosures.

Non-traditional datasets used by investors and researchers to gain analytical edges: satellite imagery, credit-card transaction records, congressional trade filings, and similar sources that fall outside standard financial statements. Firms like Quiver Quantitative aggregate and surface such data for subscribers and journalists.

article.fact_check: Quiver Quantitative's tweet cites a 376% gain on Letlow's Micron purchase made in April (year unspecified, though contextual reporting places it in 2024). Historical price data shows MU closed April 2024 at approximately $112 per share. With MU trading near $640 in early May 2026 at the time of the tweet, the actual gain from that April 2024 month-end close would be roughly 471% — higher than the 376% figure stated. The lower figure could reflect a higher intra-month purchase price (MU reached roughly $130 in late April 2024 before pulling back), a different calculation methodology, or a price snapshot taken before MU's most recent leg up. Secondary reporting from Barchart and Quiver's own site cites the gain as 'roughly 370%,' consistent with the tweet but not precisely reconcilable with end-of-month closing price data. The directional claim — a very large gain on an undisclosed position by a member of the Appropriations Committee — is well-supported; the exact percentage should be treated as approximate.

ticker_mu.name: Micron Technology, Inc.
ticker_mu.blurb: Micron is the only US-headquartered manufacturer of DRAM and NAND memory at scale, competing with Samsung and SK Hynix. Historically the most cyclical of the three, it has spent the past two years repositioning toward high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the stacked DRAM that pairs with AI accelerators, where pricing is multiples of standard DDR5 and contracts are multi-year rather than spot.
ticker_mu.recent: In March 2026 Micron began mass production of HBM4 12-Hi 36GB stacks for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform; management has stated 2026 HBM capacity is sold out under binding agreements. Fiscal Q2 2026 revenue was around $23.9 billion, with non-GAAP gross margin near 75%. The board approved a 30% dividend increase and roughly $25 billion of fiscal-2026 capex. Despite a strong year-to-date move, the forward P/E remains in the high single digits on consensus, reflecting residual cyclicality scepticism.

sources.title: Micron HBM4 in mass production for Nvidia Vera Rubin

poster_quiverquant.bio_summary: Alternative-data analytics firm that aggregates and surfaces non-traditional datasets for investors and researchers, best known for its real-time tracker of congressional stock trades scraped from STOCK Act filings. Also tracks lobbying activity, government contracts, patent filings, and other 'quiver' signals with potential market relevance. Posts breaking disclosures, late-filing alerts, and trade summaries; functions as a primary source for financial journalists covering congressional trading.
